Acute hemolytic transfusion reaction: Fever, flank pain, ↓Hb, ↑LDH, ↓haptoglobin, positive DAT, hemoglobinuria, timing ≤ 4 h — Mild – symptoms controlled with fluids; Moderate – hypotension, renal impairment; Severe – shock, disseminated intravascular coagulation, death.

qs.q: Which of the following is a sign of an acute hemolytic transfusion reaction?
qs.e: Acute hemolytic transfusion reactions can manifest with a range of symptoms including fever, chills, hypotension (low blood pressure), back pain, and dark or red-colored urine (hemoglobinuria).

faq.a: Free hemoglobin released from lysed red cells is filtered by the kidneys, giving a cola‑coloured urine.
faq.q: Why does the urine turn dark?

faq.a: Yes, if the reaction is recognised within minutes, the transfusion is stopped, fluids and vasopressors are given, and renal support is provided.
faq.q: Can a patient survive a severe AHTR?

faq.a: It confirms immune hemolysis, but in low‑resource settings a clinical picture plus rapid Hb fall may be enough to act urgently.
faq.q: Is a positive direct Coombs test always required?

exam: What is the first step when a patient develops flank pain and dark urine during a transfusion? — Stop the transfusion immediately, clamp the line, and start isotonic saline.

How would you differentiate an acute hemolytic reaction from a febrile non‑hemolytic reaction? — Hemolytic reaction shows hemoglobinuria, rapid Hb drop, low haptoglobin; febrile reaction lacks these lab changes.

A patient’s blood pressure falls to 80/50 mmHg 30 min into a transfusion. What investigations are essential next? — Send CBC, serum LDH, haptoglobin, creatinine, coagulation profile, and repeat blood typing of patient and unit.

Why is diuretics used in AHTR, and when would you avoid them? — To promote renal clearance of hemoglobin; avoid if the patient is hypovolaemic or has severe hypotension without adequate fluid resuscitation.

Explain why ABO incompatibility is the most common cause of AHTR in emergency settings. — Emergency transfusions often bypass full cross‑match; mis‑labelled or uncross‑matched blood increases the risk of ABO mismatch.
What are the key features of DIC that may develop in severe AHTR? — Prolonged PT/aPTT, low fibrinogen, high D‑dimer, thrombocytopenia, and bleeding tendency.
If the laboratory cannot perform a DAT, how should you proceed? — Base management on clinical signs (fever, hemoglobinuria, Hb fall) and stop the transfusion; arrange later confirmatory testing.

What preventive measures reduce the incidence of AHTR in low‑resource hospitals? — Strict two‑person patient ID check, bedside ABO verification, use of pre‑labelled emergency packs with known compatible blood, and regular staff training.
ai.title: Acute Hemolytic Transfusion Reaction
ai.subject: Medicine
ai.summary: A rapid, complement‑mediated intravascular hemolysis occurring within 4 h of a blood transfusion. Presents with fever, flank pain, hypotension, dark urine and a sudden fall in hemoglobin.

b: Onset within minutes to 2 h of starting the transfusion
Fever ≥38 °C, chills, flank or back pain
Dark (cola‑coloured) urine
Sudden drop in hemoglobin ≥2 g/dL or ≥20 % from baseline
sections.p: An acute hemolytic transfusion reaction is an immediate (≤4 h) intravascular destruction of donor red cells caused mainly by ABO incompatibility or other immune antibodies.

t.b: Is immune hemolysis present? – Positive DAT confirms antibody‑mediated RBC destruction
Is there intravascular hemolysis? – Undetectable or markedly low haptoglobin supports hemolysis
Is cell breakdown occurring? – Elevated LDH (>2‑times upper limit) indicates hemolysis
Is hemoglobinuria present? – Positive dipstick with no RBCs on microscopy suggests free hemoglobin

t.a: Blood group re‑typing of patient and unit
t.b: What is the compatibility error? – Mismatch confirms ABO incompatibility; if unavailable, rely on bedside cross‑match records

b: Mild – fever, chills, flank pain; stable vitals; no renal impairment
Moderate – hypotension (SBP <90 mmHg), oliguria, rising creatinine
Severe – shock, disseminated intravascular coagulation (DIC), renal failure, death
sections.p: The reaction is graded by clinical impact and organ dysfunction.

b: ABO incompatibility (most common, especially in emergency or mislabeled units)
Other alloantibodies (anti‑D, anti‑K, etc.)
Clerical errors – wrong patient identification, sample mix‑up
Cold agglutinins or complement‑fixing antibodies in patients with malaria, sickle cell disease, or recent infections
sections.p: Most AHTRs are immune mediated; non‑immune causes are rare in low‑resource settings.

b: Fever and chills
Severe retro‑orbital or flank pain
Hypotension, tachycardia
Dark urine (hemoglobinuria)
Rapid fall in hemoglobin and rise in LDH
sections.p: Symptoms appear abruptly after the transfusion starts and progress over minutes.
Focus on confirming hemolysis, identifying the incompatibility, and assessing organ injury.

t.b: How much has the patient lost? – Drop ≥2 g/dL or ≥20 % signals significant hemolysis
Is the kidney injured? – Rising creatinine or oliguria (<0.5 mL/kg/h) indicates renal compromise
Is DIC developing? – Prolonged PT/aPTT, low fibrinogen, high D‑dimer suggest DIC
What to do? – Rely on clinical picture, stop transfusion, give fluids, and send blood samples for later testing

b: Unexplained hypotension or shock
Rapidly decreasing urine output
Laboratory evidence of DIC
Persistent fever >38 °C after transfusion stop
Stop the blood bag and clamp the line; keep IV access with normal saline
Give rapid isotonic crystalloids (e.g., 0.9 % saline) to maintain perfusion and promote renal clearance of hemoglobin
Consider diuretics (e.g., furosemide) if urine output is low and no contraindication
Treat hypotension with vasopressors (e.g., norepinephrine) if fluids insufficient
If DIC develops, give fresh frozen plasma and platelets; avoid heparin unless thrombosis dominates
Monitor vitals, urine output, labs every 30 min for the first 2 h
sections.p: Immediate cessation of the transfusion, supportive care, and treatment of complications.

b: Document the incompatibility and notify the blood bank
Re‑type patient and cross‑match a new unit before any further transfusion
Implement double‑check patient ID and bedside cross‑match protocols
Educate on proper labeling, especially in emergency wards where rapid transfusion is common
sections.p: After stabilization, investigate the error and educate staff.

b: Febrile non‑hemolytic reaction – fever only, no hemoglobinuria or drop in Hb
Allergic reaction – urticaria, itching, no hemolysis
Transfusion‑related acute lung injury (TRALI) – respiratory distress, bilateral infiltrates, no hemoglobinuria
sections.p: Other transfusion reactions may mimic early AHTR.

b: Haptoglobin may remain detectable early; repeat if suspicion persists
Urine dipstick can be positive for blood from myoglobin (e.g., rhabdomyolysis); microscopy distinguishes RBCs from free hemoglobin
sections.p: Certain labs may be falsely reassuring.

whenToSeekHelp: Rapid fall in urine output (<0.5 mL/kg/h)
Signs of DIC (bleeding, bruising, prolonged clotting times)
